newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Euro stocks slip lower, dollar holds ground.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Euro stocks slip lower, dollar holds ground.

text.p: European stock markets slipped lower on Friday morning, subdued by a weak finish in New York, where the Dow continued to fall on warnings by U.S. Federal Reserve head Alan Greenspan.

In Frankfurt the DAX index dropped from Thursday's record high and German shares extended early losses in nervous trading amid speculation that the launch of European economic and monetary union (EMU) was to be delayed.
But the Bundesbank and German Finance Ministry denied a market rumour that Germany was about to issue a statement saying EMU would be delayed.

"Speculation that the Bundesbank plans to make a statement on a delay in EMU is complete nonsense," a spokesman for the central bank said, adding, "We are not aware of any intentions which go in this direction."
The dollar opened firmly against the mark in European trading and analysts said they expected it to remain robust amid a lack of fresh factors since economic fundamentals favoured the United States.

"There is the reflection, as far as investors are concerned, that if you're not going to buy dollars then where are you going to put your money?" said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist for Europe at BankAmerica here.
But continued repatriation of funds by Japanese firms ahead of their financial year-end in March should continue to keep a cap on dollar/yen trade, they added.
A series of U.S. data, due out later on Friday, was also expected to underline the healthiness of the U.S. economy, analysts said.

The drop on Wall Street helped prompt the London stock market, Europe's busiest, to fall around three-quarters of a percentage point in early trading, while sterling initially lost ground after a parliamentary by-election in which the ruling Conservative Party suffered a crushing defeat.

But markets had expected a win by the opposition Labour Party in the by-election -- and in a general election due by May -- and analysts said any downward move for the pound should be temporary. Sterling soon revived from its lows.

"The effect of the by-election should not have a large impact because the unpopularity of the current government is hardly a surprise," said Klaus Baader, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell
Although many investors are traditionally pro-Conservative, a clear-cut victory by Labour would be welcomed more than the possibility of uncertainty or a hung parliament after the general election.
Analysts said the market should be relieved that the by-election result could allay such fears.
"The market was expecting the worst in the by-election, and that is what we got," a London share dealer added.

French share dealers said their market's weak start was on the back of the Dow Jones Industrial Index's 58-point fall overnight but it had the potential to move higher, supported by a firm tone to bonds and the dollar.
Meanwhile, on the bullion market, platinum was fixed at $398.75 per ounce, its highest since August 29, 1996, boosting gold in its wake.
Dealers said platinum's gains from Thursday's close of $386.00/$387.00 were driven by buying in Tokyo on concern about delays in Russian supplies.
CURRENCIES AT 1100 GMT
The dollar was at 1.6920 marks and 120.50 yen, compared with 1.6892 and 120.70 in late European trade on Thursday.
Sterling traded around 2.7550 marks and $1.6290 versus 2.7484 and $1.6266 overnight.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1100 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was down 33.1 points at 4,306.1.
PARIS - The CAC-40 fell 17.15 points at 2,612.25.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was 21.04 points lower at 3,255.68.
PRECIOUS METALS

Gold was fixed at $360.60, up 60 cents and at its highest since January 3, boosted by strength in platinum. Silver added two cents to $5.27. Platinum was fixed at fresh high of $398.75 after heavy buying.
